slides.text: An AI wrote this, and it passes the sample ([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3 → 9). Would you ship it?
slides.alt: Python max_sum_k(nums, k) tagged "AI · passes the sample": best = float("-inf"); for i in range(len(nums) - k): best = max(best, sum(nums[i:i + k])); return best. Under it [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3 → 9 ✓, with the windows walked on the array.

slides.text: Count the windows: a 2-wide frame on 4 numbers fits at starts 0, 1 and 2. That's n − k + 1.
slides.alt: "Count the windows": a 2-wide frame on 1, 2, 3, 9 fits at start 0, start 1 and start 2, with the last one, 3 and 9, lit.

slides.text: range(n − k) stops one short, so the last window is never checked. Fix: + 1.
slides.alt: The same code with for i in range(len(nums) - k): highlighted and the note "Start 2, [3, 9]: never checked"; on 1, 2, 3, 9 the pair 3, 9 is ringed: start 2: 3 + 9 = 12, never checked.

slides.text: Slide instead: sum the first window once, then add the number entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left. O(n).
slides.alt: The sliding version: window = sum(nums[:k]); best = window; for right in range(k, len(nums)): window += nums[right] - nums[right - k]; best = max(best, window), with that line highlighted and the note "Keep the best". On 2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2 with k = 3: +3 − 1 → window 9, best 9.

slides.text: Our test run, 100,000 numbers with k = 10,000 (Python): 12.35 s summing every window vs 11.7 ms sliding.
slides.alt: "100,000 numbers, k = 10,000, our test run, Python": summing every window (with the +1 fix) takes 12.35 s; sliding the sum takes 11.7 ms.
